newsitem.title: MONACO: Lloyd's needs marketing skills to regain status.
newsitem.headline: Lloyd's needs marketing skills to regain status.

text.p: Underwriters in the Lloyd's of London insurance market are under pressure to become more active in marketing their wares to potential buyers.
Last week the market saw the acceptance of its Reconstruction and Renewal plan, which gave Names a 3.2 billion stg settlement and formed the Equitas reinsurance company to assume old liabilities.

Having put the worst of its problems behind it, the market should now be in a position to regain some of the ground it lost while it was engulfed by massive losses and high-profile litigation with Names in the UK and U.S.
But many analysts and rival market practitioners are sceptical as to whether Lloyd's has the marketing skills to rebuild the tarnished reputation of the market in the eyes of clients.

In recent years major European insurers and reinsurers such as Zurich and Munich Re have developed much closer relationships with their insureds, and brokers have had to look for ways of providing added value to the service they provide.
But underwriters at Lloyd's have remained heavily reliant on brokers.

"I can understand Lloyd's underwriters not wanting to have to explain what (chairman David) Rowland was up to with the problems of the past. They were right to keep a low profile," said Roger Morgan, deputy chairman of the LIMIT corporate capital vehicle.
"But as of this week underwriters should be getting on their planes to sell their story to buyers," he said.
To some extent these criticisms are being answered by an exercise Lloyd's is calling meet the markets.

On September 20, Rowland will lead a group of 50 to 60 brokers and underwriters on a U.S. roadshow visiting New York, Chicago and Los Angeles. The week long tour is aimed at highlighting the things Lloyd's is good at -- innovation, flexibility and highly professional underwriting.

But critics of the market at the Monte Carlo rendezvous said that, although the idea was laudable, it was a Corporation initiative which reflects the marketing awareness of Rowland and his team rather than that of the underwriters themselves.
"Rowland is a brilliant ambassador, but he is not an underwriter and he still has an association with the past," said one critic.
"This meeting in Monaco is the greatest concentration of reinsurers and brokers in the world, but how many underwriters from Lloyd's are here. Barely a handful," he said.
Rowland accepts that underwriters need to go out and get new business, and has said he would like to see more at Monte Carlo.
"This is a grossly inefficient business, so there are huge advantages to be gained by those who improve the inefficiency of it," he told Reuters.

But he also spelled out his view of the role the Corporation should take on the marketing side. "I want the market to tell me where I should be going, who I should be speaking to. I am its tool, that is what I'm there for," he said.
